hello.note: The easy hello visitors hear everywhere. Between locals it's Hujambo? (hoo-JAHM-boh), answered Sijambo (see-JAHM-boh). To an older person, Shikamoo (shee-kah-MOH), answered Marahaba

how-are-you.note: Literally "your news?" The answer is always good, nzuri (n-ZOO-ree), whatever the news

good-morning.note: Literally "news of the morning?" The reply is nzuri

good-night.note: Literally "sleep in peace". Usiku mwema (oo-SEE-koo MWEH-mah) is a good night when parting

goodbye.note: To more than one person, kwaherini (kwah-heh-REE-nee)

please.note: The dh is the th in "this"

thank-you.note: Asante sana (SAH-nah) means thank you very much

youre-welcome.note: Also welcome, and come in. You'll hear it everywhere

no.note: Hapana, asante is a polite no thank you to a seller

excuse-me.note: Sorry, and excuse me to get attention. At a door, call Hodi! (HOH-dee) and wait for Karibu

my-name.note: The audio uses Peter as the example name

its-beautiful.note: For a place. For a thing, ni nzuri sana

speak-slowly.note: Polepole (slowly, gently) is a whole way of life on the coast

speak-english.note: English is widely spoken in Kenya, less so in rural Tanzania

four.note: Two n's: hum the first, then say neh

thousand.note: Prices are in shillings, shilingi: Kenyan (KSh) or Tanzanian (TSh), worth very different amounts

hundred-thousand.note: Swahili has its own word for a hundred thousand, laki

how-much.note: Literally "what price?" Point at the thing

would-like.note: Literally "I request", the polite way to ask for anything. The audio uses kahawa (kah-HAH-wah), coffee, as the example

i-want.note: More direct than naomba. The audio uses hii (HEE), this one, as the example

do-you-have.note: Literally "is there...?", the usual way to ask in a shop. The audio uses maji (MAH-jee), water, as the example

too-expensive.note: The gh is a soft gargle, like French r

discount.note: Literally "lower it a little, please". Bargaining is normal in markets and with souvenir sellers; keep it friendly

card.note: Cards work in hotels and bigger shops. Elsewhere it's cash or mobile money, M-Pesa

checkout-time.note: Swahili time starts at dawn: saa moja, the first hour, is 7 am. Check whether a time is Swahili or English time

breakfast.note: Literally "the mouth-opener, is it there?" Kifungua kinywa is breakfast

taxi.note: Agree the fare first, or use a ride app. Motorbike taxis are boda boda in Kenya and bodaboda or piki piki in Tanzania

train.note: The fast SGR trains run Nairobi to Mombasa in Kenya and Dar es Salaam to Dodoma in Tanzania

bus.note: Shared minibuses are matatu in Kenya and dala dala in Tanzania

which-train.note: Literally "which train goes ...?" The audio uses Mombasa as the example

two-tickets.note: Kwenda (KWEN-dah) means to go. The audio uses Mombasa as the example
two-tickets.spoken: Tiketi mbili za kwenda Mombasa, tafadhali

trip-length.text: Safari ya kwenda... inachukua muda gani?
trip-length.say: sah-FAH-ree yah KWEN-dah ... ee-nah-choo-KOO-ah MOO-dah GAH-nee
trip-length.note: Safari is simply Swahili for journey. The audio uses Mombasa
trip-length.spoken: Safari ya kwenda Mombasa inachukua muda gani?
trip-length.filled: Safari ya kwenda ⟦Mombasa⟧ inachukua muda gani?

allergic.note: Add the food: samaki (sah-MAH-kee) fish, karanga (kah-RAHN-gah) peanuts, mayai (mah-YAH-ee) eggs. The audio uses peanuts

love-dish.note: Literally "I like this food very much"

what-called.note: Point at the dish or item

table-for-two.note: For more people: watatu (wah-TAH-too), 3, or wanne (WAHN-neh), 4

beer.note: Ask for baridi, cold, as beer can come warm. Tusker, Kilimanjaro and Safari are the local beers

coffee.note: On the coast, tiny cups of strong kahawa are sold in the street

tea.note: Usually milky and sweet, often with spices. Black tea is chai ya rangi

hot.note: Hot, and also fire. Hot weather is joto (JOH-toh). Spicy is pilipili, from the pepper

cold.note: Cold, of drinks and of the weather

help.note: Shout it. In Kenya call 999 or 112; in Tanzania, 112

need-doctor.note: For an ambulance, call 999 or 112 in Kenya, 114 or 112 in Tanzania

pharmacy.note: Literally "the medicine shop". Pharmacy and chemist are widely understood
